operations.evidence: Court proceedings data are supplied by the Crown Prosecution Service Counter Terrorism Division and cover completed cases from year ending March 2011 to March 2026.
The series covers completed court cases rather than all arrests.
Sentence-length breakdowns for defendants tried and convicted after March 2024 are excluded because the data were unavailable to the Home Office.
The missing breakdown limits sentence trend analysis.
The 93% conviction rate was the second highest for a year ending March since comparable records began in March 2010.
Historical rank is conditional on cases tried and not a general crime rate.
Court data use the principal-offence basis, showing the most serious offence with the largest sentence when a person is tried for multiple offences.
Counts therefore do not represent every charge or offence in a trial.
Section 58 of the Terrorism Act 2000 had 17 convictions, the largest listed principal-offence count.
Principal-offence counts omit additional offences in multi-offence trials.
Section 2 of the Terrorism Act 2006 had 10 convictions for dissemination of terrorist publications.
This court aggregate cannot identify local public-safety conditions.
Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006 had 8 convictions for preparation of terrorist acts.
The count is national court data, not a parcel risk score.
Schedule 7 of the Terrorism Act 2000 had 7 convictions as the principal offence.
Principal-offence statistics must not be interpreted as incident locations.
The 273 persons in custody on 31 March 2026 was the highest total since comparable records began and exceeded the previous peak of 267 at 31 December 2025.
Custody levels are system-wide and not local exposure measures.
Of the 273 in custody, 159 were categorised as Islamist-extremist, 80 as Extreme Right-Wing and 34 as Other ideologies.
Institutional ideology categories must not be used to profile communities, individuals or parcels.
Forty-one terrorist prisoners were released in the year ending 31 December 2025, compared with 50 in the previous year.
Release totals are national and do not identify release destinations or local risk.
Of 41 releases, 17 had sentences under four years, 21 had sentences of four years or more, none were released from IPP or life sentences, and 3 had been convicted but not sentenced.
Sentence history does not identify an individual's destination or parcel-level risk.
Section 43 search and arrest figures for forces outside the MPS are published as Official Statistics in Development because of identified data-quality issues.
These figures should not be used for precise force-to-force or parcel comparisons.
There were 2,614 Schedule 7 examinations in Great Britain, 14% more than the 2,290 in the previous year.
Examinations are not arrests or convictions and do not measure parcel risk.
Fifty-three percent of UK Schedule 7 examinations involved at least one biometric identifier, covering 1,436 persons out of 2,714 examinations.
The UK denominator differs from the Great Britain examination total and must not be mixed without care.
Eight strip searches were carried out under Schedule 7 powers in the year ending 31 March 2026.
A small national procedural count cannot support local inference.
There were 566 air freight examinations, 41% fewer than in the previous year.
Freight examinations are operational activity and not parcel-level public-safety evidence.
There were 302 sea freight examinations, 92% more than in the previous year.
The national change does not describe risk at a property.
There were no refusals to postpone questioning for solicitor consultation and three instances of delayed solicitor access.
Procedural safeguards data are not measures of neighbourhood safety.
For non-MPS section 43 records, 5% had the reason for a resultant arrest recorded as not stated and 19% had self-defined ethnicity not stated or missing.
The missingness varies between forces and prevents precise demographic or parcel-level comparisons.
